body:
Nuclear energy comes from changes in atomic nuclei

Nuclear reactions involve the nuclei of atoms, not merely the rearrangement of electrons that occurs in ordinary chemical reactions. Certain nuclear changes release large amounts of energy because a small difference in mass corresponds to released energy.

The two fundamental nuclear processes relevant to elementary science are nuclear fission and nuclear fusion. Both involve nuclear transformations, but their directions are opposite.

Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus into smaller nuclei, usually accompanied by the release of neutrons and energy.

Uranium-235 is a familiar example of a fissile isotope. When its nucleus absorbs a suitable neutron, it may split into smaller nuclei. Energy and additional neutrons are released. Some of these neutrons can cause further fission events.

This continuation is called a chain reaction. In a nuclear power reactor, the reaction is controlled so that nuclear energy can be released steadily as heat.

Fission is not the same as ordinary radioactive decay. Radioactive decay is spontaneous transformation of an unstable nucleus, whereas the usual power-reactor example of uranium-235 fission is initiated by neutron absorption. Some heavy nuclei can also undergo spontaneous fission.

Nuclear fusion joins light nuclei

Nuclear fusion is the joining of light atomic nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, with energy released in suitable reactions.

Fusion reactions power the Sun and other stars. In the Sun, a sequence of nuclear reactions ultimately converts hydrogen into helium and releases energy. Fusion requires extremely demanding conditions because positively charged nuclei repel one another.

Deuterium and tritium, the heavier isotopes of hydrogen, are also important in fusion research. However, commercial nuclear electricity generation currently relies on fission, not fusion. Fusion remains an area of technological development.

FeatureFissionFusion
Basic changeHeavy nucleus splitsLight nuclei combine
Typical exampleUranium-235Hydrogen nuclei forming helium
Familiar settingNuclear power reactorSun and stars
Electricity generationUsed in commercial nuclear plantsNot yet used for routine commercial grid generation

How a nuclear power station generates electricity

A nuclear power plant is a thermal power station in which fission supplies the heat. It does not convert nuclear radiation directly into the electricity supplied to homes.

  1. Controlled fission releases heat in the reactor.
  2. A coolant transfers the heat, which is used to produce steam.
  3. Steam drives a turbine.
  4. The turbine rotates an electrical generator.
  5. The generator produces electricity for transmission to users.

Reactor arrangements differ in how heat is transferred and steam is produced, but the basic energy-conversion principle remains the same: nuclear energy to heat, mechanical energy and electrical energy.

Nuclear plants can produce substantial electricity with relatively low direct carbon dioxide emissions during operation. They also require strict radiation protection, cooling arrangements, management of radioactive waste and long-term safety oversight. The presence of uranium fuel does not mean that a nuclear reactor operates by fusion.

Kakrapar Atomic Power Station: the Gujarat connection

The Kakrapar Atomic Power Station (KAPS) is located near Surat in Gujarat. It is operated by the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL). Its operating units are pressurised heavy water reactors, commonly abbreviated PHWR.

According to NPCIL's operating information available at the 3 November 2026 content cutoff, with generation statistics reported for April-August 2026, Kakrapar has the following 4 commercially operating units:

UnitCapacity (MWe)Commercial operation began
KAPS-12206 May 1993
KAPS-22201 September 1995
KAPS-370030 June 2023
KAPS-470031 March 2024

The combined installed electrical capacity of these units is 1840 MWe. The figure is a measure of rated electrical generating capacity, not the amount of electricity produced in a year. Units 3 and 4 belong to India's indigenous 700 MWe PHWR programme.

Prelims focus

  • Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion combines light nuclei.
  • Uranium-235 is a familiar fission fuel.
  • Fusion powers the Sun; commercial nuclear power plants use fission.
  • Nuclear electricity is generated through heat, steam, turbine and generator.
  • Kakrapar is in Gujarat and is operated by NPCIL.
  • As recorded at the cutoff, KAPS has 4 commercially operating units with a combined capacity of 1840 MWe.
  • Trap: Nuclear power plants do not ordinarily obtain grid electricity by directly collecting gamma rays.

[US Department of Energy, Office of Nuclear Energy, Fission and Fusion: What Is the Difference?, 1 April 2021, sections on fission and fusion, consulted 3 November 2026; Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, Operating Performance: Kakrapar Atomic Power Station, unit details and April-August 2026 generation period, consulted 3 November 2026; NPCIL, Reactors in Operation, Kakrapar entries, consulted 3 November 2026.]

body:
Why radiation has medical value

Ionising radiation can pass through some materials and can interact with living tissues. These properties make it useful in medicine. A suitably chosen amount of radiation can help reveal internal structures or physiological activity. A therapeutic dose can damage selected diseased cells, including cancer cells.

The benefit depends on choosing the appropriate examination or treatment, while protecting the patient, healthcare workers and others from unnecessary exposure.

Diagnostic X-rays and CT scans

X-rays are electromagnetic radiation. In a conventional medical X-ray machine, they are generated electrically rather than emitted by a radioactive substance placed inside the patient.

Different tissues absorb X-rays to different extents. This difference helps produce images of structures such as bones. A CT scan also uses X-rays, but combines information collected from different directions to produce cross-sectional images.

An X-ray examination does not ordinarily make the patient radioactive. Receiving radiation from a machine is different from having radioactive material inside or on the body.

Nuclear medicine uses radioactive tracers

In nuclear medicine, a patient receives a carefully selected radioactive substance, called a radiopharmaceutical, for diagnosis or treatment. The radioactive component emits detectable radiation. The substance's chemical behaviour helps determine where it travels or accumulates in the body.

Diagnostic nuclear medicine therefore provides information about the function or activity of tissues, not only their external shape. Gamma cameras and related imaging systems can detect signals associated with radiopharmaceuticals.

Technetium-99m is widely used in diagnostic nuclear medicine. Fluorine-18 is used in PET imaging. The radioisotope and procedure are chosen according to the clinical purpose.

Radiotherapy uses radiation to treat disease

Radiotherapy uses ionising radiation to damage cells in a targeted area, particularly in cancer treatment. The aim is to deliver an effective dose to diseased tissue while limiting the dose received by surrounding healthy tissues.

Cobalt-60 emits gamma radiation and has been used as a source in external-beam radiotherapy. Modern radiotherapy can also use radiation generated by machines. Consequently, radiotherapy does not always require a radioactive source.

Iodine-131 is a radioactive isotope used in particular thyroid treatments. Its usefulness arises partly because iodine is taken up by thyroid tissue. It is not a general treatment for every form of goitre or thyroid disease.

Medical applicationMain principleExample
Diagnostic radiographyExternal X-rays form an image through differential absorptionBone X-ray
Diagnostic nuclear medicineRadiation from a tracer is detectedTechnetium-99m imaging
RadiotherapyTargeted ionising radiation damages diseased cellsCobalt-60 cancer treatment
Radioisotope therapyA radioactive substance delivers radiation to selected tissueIodine-131 thyroid treatment

Radiation safety: exposure and contamination

Radiation exposure occurs when radiation reaches a person. Radioactive contamination occurs when radioactive material is deposited on or enters a person or object. A person may be exposed to radiation without becoming contaminated.

Protection against external radiation relies on 3 basic principles:

  • Time: Limit unnecessary time near a radiation source.
  • Distance: Increasing distance from an external source generally reduces exposure.
  • Shielding: Use appropriate barriers for the radiation involved.

Preventing radioactive material from being inhaled, swallowed or spread onto surfaces is additionally important when working with unsealed radioactive substances. The correct protective measure depends on the type of radiation and how exposure could occur.

In India, the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) regulates radiation safety in relevant medical facilities. Clinical radiation procedures are justified by their expected medical benefit and undertaken with appropriate dose control.

Prelims focus

  • X-rays and gamma rays are forms of electromagnetic ionising radiation.
  • Diagnostic X-ray machines generate X-rays electrically.
  • Technetium-99m is a diagnostic nuclear medicine isotope.
  • Cobalt-60 is associated with cancer radiotherapy.
  • Iodine-131 is used in selected thyroid treatments.
  • Time, distance and shielding are basic principles of external radiation protection.
  • Trap: Exposure to radiation and contamination by radioactive material are different.

[Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Nuclear Medicine, sections on diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals, consulted 3 November 2026; AERB, I Am a Patient, sections on nuclear medicine and patient radiation protection, consulted 3 November 2026; AERB, Annual Report 2019, section 2.2.1, Medical Applications of Radiation Sources; UK Government, Basic Concepts of Radiation, sections on radiation types and health effects, consulted 3 November 2026.]

body:
Electrical conductivity depends on moving charge

Electric current is the movement of electric charge. Different materials permit this movement to different extents because their charged particles are not equally free to move.

A material that allows electric current to pass easily is called an electrical conductor. A material that strongly resists current is called an electrical insulator. A semiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity can be controlled substantially by factors such as added impurities, temperature and illumination.

Material groupTypical examplesImportant use
ConductorsCopper, aluminium, silverElectrical connections and wiring
InsulatorsRubber, plastic, glass, dry woodElectrical separation and protection
SemiconductorsSilicon, germaniumDiodes, transistors and electronic circuits

Why metals usually conduct well

Metals contain electrons that can move through the material. When an electric field is applied, these mobile electrons contribute to electric current. Copper and aluminium are widely used as conductors because they combine useful electrical conductivity with practical properties.

A metal wire is commonly covered with an insulating material so that current follows the intended path rather than passing through a person or another nearby conductor.

Not every non-metal is an electrical insulator. Graphite, a form of carbon, conducts electricity despite being a non-metal. This exception shows why conductivity should not be identified merely by the words metal and non-metal.

Insulators resist the movement of charge

In materials such as rubber and many plastics, electrons are not readily available to move through the substance under ordinary conditions. These materials are therefore useful as insulators.

However, insulation is not absolute under every possible condition. Very high electric fields, moisture, contamination or damage can cause a normally insulating material or surface to conduct. Air is generally a poor conductor under ordinary conditions, but an electric discharge can occur through air during lightning.

The words conductor and insulator describe how a material behaves under specified conditions. They do not guarantee that current will always flow or never flow.

Electrical conduction in liquids

Current in metals is mainly carried by electrons. In conducting solutions, current is carried substantially by moving ions, which are electrically charged atoms or groups of atoms.

Pure distilled water is a very poor electrical conductor. When substances such as common salt dissolve in water and form mobile ions, the resulting solution conducts electricity much better. Tap water also commonly contains dissolved ions.

Therefore, water containing dissolved salts can present an electrical hazard even though water itself is not a metal. A weakly conducting material may allow some current to flow without producing enough current to light an ordinary filament bulb.

What makes a semiconductor special?

In a semiconductor such as silicon, electrical conduction can occur through moving electrons and through holes. A hole represents a missing electron in a place where an electron could otherwise be present. When nearby electrons move to fill such vacancies, the holes behave as positively charged carriers for describing current.

In an ordinary intrinsic semiconductor, an increase in temperature generally makes more charge carriers available, so conductivity tends to increase. Metals commonly show the opposite trend: their electrical resistance generally increases as temperature rises because moving electrons encounter more scattering.

This comparison concerns ordinary temperature ranges and typical material behaviour. It is not a universal rule that every conductor or every semiconductor must respond in precisely the same way under all conditions.

Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors

A pure semiconductor is called an intrinsic semiconductor. Its electrical behaviour comes from the semiconductor material itself.

When carefully selected impurity atoms are added to change its electrical properties, the material is called an extrinsic semiconductor. This intentional addition is called doping. Doping does not mean ordinary dirt or accidental contamination; it means controlled addition of suitable atoms.

The ability to control conduction is what makes semiconductors central to electronic devices. Metals are usually selected to carry current efficiently, while semiconductors are often selected to control when and how current flows.

Prelims focus

  • Copper and aluminium are familiar electrical conductors.
  • Rubber, plastic and glass are commonly used as electrical insulators.
  • Silicon and germanium are semiconductors.
  • Graphite is a conducting form of carbon.
  • Dissolved ions make salt solutions electrically conducting.
  • Intrinsic means undoped; extrinsic means intentionally doped.
  • Trap: Semiconductors are not merely poor conductors; their conductivity can be deliberately controlled.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 12, Electricity and Circuits, printed pp. 121-123; NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 14, Chemical Effects of Electric Current, printed pp. 172-176; OpenStax, Physics, section 18.1, Electrical Charges, Conservation of Charge, and Transfer of Charge, consulted 3 November 2026; OpenStax, University Physics Volume 3, section 9.6, Semiconductors and Doping, consulted 3 November 2026.]
